items.title: Show HN: Caudra – An open-source terminal coding agent in one native binary
items.summary: Hi all, Thorsten from Caudra ( https://caudra.ai ) here. I'm building Caudra, an open source coding agent written in Rust with a good, albeit opinionated, experience out-of-the-box. You don't need mess with plugins or keep them up-to-date. As a software engineer/data architect, I spend most of my day with coding agents and i tried many of them. I needed something that combines all the great features of these agents + new features in a new standalone TUI binary that i can easily get up running in new environments. I also needed something that works great with small models (including local ones) as well as with flagship models. Caudra does a lot of hand-holding and context management automatically so agents stay on track. QoL improvements: It supports eager streaming so you don't need to wait on a spinning icon and directly see how tool calls are being formed. Subagents are interactive as soon as possible (already after the first instruction token is being streamed). Define goals (like in claude code) to make sure that the agent actually works toward it without going astray. Continual learning: a background agent that automatically remembers important details and quirks in your setup, the way you desire things, and saves them in your AGENTS.md, AGENTS.local.md, global AGENTS.md, and memory system. Three message steering types: "next" waits until user turn, "guide" sends at the next safe boundary (like most coding agents), "replace" inserts now. "next" is really cool because it only sends the message once the turn is completely over (allows some really rudimentary ad-hoc chains). Autopilot can answer permissions prompts and questions for you and makes sure the agent is not stalled before reaching (or failing) a goal. Caudra nudges the model: stalled turns (particularly useful for smaller models like Qwen-3.8-27b that sometimes just stop at turns), nudge to use question tool when models ends a turn which could more easily be handled by just answering question prompt (requires decision model to be configured). Integrates well with Herdr and Orca you might be already using, proper support for git worktrees, (git-based) automatic workspace snapshots. Markdown rendering including math and mermaid charts (common ones). /btw lets you always ask side questions (including follow-ups with almost 100% cache hits) without interrupting the main agent (can even be used during an active question tool prompt to ask for more context). Token savings: Even though many things can be hot (re)loaded, they never break the provider prompt cache (conversations are append only). This results in pretty good provider cache rates: anthropic models ~97% (98% with cache warming) and openai models ~94%. Background (async) subagents and tasks turn Caudra into an event driven coding agent. This results in faster throughput and more provider cache hits (caches are still warm). Deferred questions let you answer some questions at your convenience without blocking the main agent. Code mode runs Monty Python in a separate process: all configured MCP resources are exposed here as well as some of Caudra's internal tools that shouldn't always stay armed in system context. Efficient (infinite-like) memory system (with good recalls), RTK-like token reductions (from shell outputs), file index and source code context/refs tools (similarly to ripwire) to efficiently navigate codebases. Permissions and security: Decomposes complex commands e.g. `make lint && make test` are really two different commands (can learn and detect permission patterns as well). Built-in decision engine (JEV and OpenAI decision compatible) for content screening, shell effects, re-ranking, etc. Only forwards safe or whitelisted environment variables to shell tool. By default doesn't let you fetch loopback or LAN IPs unless you allow it. This was really just the tip of the iceberg. Have fun trying it out.

items.summary: If you use AI to create images and videos, you most likely use Higgsfield or similar subscription tools. I did too. But I had 3 main issues with it: The markup is super high. So if the model provider charges x, higgsfield charges a markup of + 50% on top. Credits I did not use would expire every month....EVEN THOUGH I PAID FOR IT And I had to switch between Claude and Higgsfield constantly...copy pasting prompts and all So I built a free open source repo of creative production skills for AI agents. So basically, you just install this skill package in Claude (or any agent you use) and say "Create a summer sale UGC video for my product". And it handles the rest. You obviously stay in control all along. And: You can use your own API keys...which adds ZERO markup on the model provider costs There is no subscription. You only pay for what you use and nothing EXPIRES And no more switching between tools and no more copy pasting We are releasing the skills in batches. The Kessler Syndrome (where blowups multiply exponentially) applied to software
items.summary: Earlier this year, inspired by a spate of supply chain attacks (like Mini Shai-Hulud-style worms, which culminated in headlines like Microsoft's Azure tools themselves being compromised), I wrote on my blog about the Kessler Syndrome, applied to software. Ie: the rising likelihood that, because of how bad actors with agentic AI can do far more damage, more quickly with the secrets they exfiltrate from penetrated networks, we could get into a situation where essentially every network of medium or greater complexity would become permanently "tainted" (never fully clean). Basically, can a swarm of agents 1) penetrate networks and exfiltrate secrets, 2) successfully install deeply embedded malware/rootkits, 3) move on to the next network, faster than hugops teams can rotate secrets and restore servers cleanly? For basically the entire existence of networked computers, this would have seemed a fantastical notion. But, throw in the current AI-fueled exploit discoveries and the countless servers vulnerable to RCEs across several stacks: I feel like the probability just keeps rising. Here are excerpts from my blog post, June 10: "'The Kessler Syndrome is a scenario where the density of objects and space debris in low Earth orbit becomes so high that collisions between them trigger a runaway chain reaction. Each crash generates thousands of new fragments, exponentially increasing the risk of further impacts and potentially rendering Earth’s orbit unusable.' "Just counting some of the high profile examples of public repos being laced with malware lately: Microsoft just disabled 70+ of their own repos, including Azure building tools. Repos from RedHat, tanstack, axios, Mistral, UiPath, and many other lower profile targets have been hacked. The list is long, and is much longer if you count companies (not just public repos for devs) that have been bitten, including names like GitHub, Cisco, OpenAI, and more. "...AIs or fancy new systems, probably made with AI appear to have dramatically lowered the amount of time to first utilization of stolen credentials. "It takes too long to clean an infected system/network (and the malware is getting much smarter/vindictive about detecting its removal, further complicating things), and it takes almost no time for a batch of stolen credentials to be exploited -> new networks traversed, leading to more secrets (that likely compromise more projects, rinse and repeat). "I think there is the very real possibility that we reach a Kessler Syndrome situation for shared/open source software, where the success of continued credential stealing campaigns permanently compromises medium, large, and even small networks, and lowers trust in shared software to a crippling degree." In just October: > Railway - customer secrets exposure > LiteLLM - malicious PyPI + Docker releases > Zeabur - infrastructure breached > OpenCode - AI API keys exposed > OVHcloud CLI - official binaries backdoored > Rank Math PRO - malware in official plugin > TeamUpdraft - customer data compromised > ConnectWise - cloud backup identities compromised > Tensorlake - npm package infected > PingCap - alleged major breach > SubQuery - backdoored npm package > GhostAction - GitHub repos with malicious workflows > PHP - critical RCE flaws > Node.js - security flaws patched > eMudhra - certificate authority keys compromised > Tailscale - eMudhra incident
